topic: ERC-8183 "Agentic Commerce" — specification text and verification of the APEX deployment on BNB Smart Chain (chain 56)
executive_summary:
ERC-8183 exists and is real. eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8183 serves it as Draft, Standards Track / ERC, created 2026-02-25, Requires: EIP-20, authors Davide Crapis, Bryan Lim, Tay Weixiong, Chooi Zuhwa, discussion at ethereum-magicians.org/t/erc-8183-agentic-commerce/27902. The prior research is confirmed on every point checked (JobStatus enum, lifecycle verbs, IACPHook.beforeAction/afterAction) and extended: Requires EIP-20, a `Job` struct with an `expiredAt` field and an optional per-job `hook`, nine custom errors, ERC-2771 meta-tx support, optional platform+evaluator fees deducted only on completion, and a RECOMMENDED (not required) integration with ERC-8004 for reputation.

The deployment is REAL and BUSY, verified by direct eth_call against BSC public RPC — not by trusting the README. All four addresses hold code. 0xEa4DAa31… is an ERC-1967/UUPS proxy (impl 0xd5f9b570c96b5d67702d508c0bfb8b3b09209787) whose runtime bytecode contains the exact ERC-8183 selectors for createJob, setBudget, submit, complete, reject, claimRefund, getJob. `paymentToken()` returns 0xcE2443…666666, which is a transparent proxy for an ERC-20 named "United Stables", symbol "U", 18 decimals, ~1.0198e9 total supply. Job IDs are sequential; binary search puts the highest live job at **56610**, and job 56610 was submitted 2026-08-18T11:54:17Z — i.e. hours before this report. Most jobs carry evaluator = 0x51895229… (the EvaluatorRouter), so the router is the on-chain evaluator of record and also implements beforeAction/afterAction — it *is* the IACPHook.

Two divergences matter for AiKi: deployed `fund(uint256,uint256,bytes)` and `setProvider(uint256,address,bytes)` differ from the spec's `fund(uint256,bytes)` / `setProvider(uint256,address)`. Build against the deployed ABI, not the EIP text. BscScan source-verification status could not be established (Cloudflare 403 on WebFetch and on headless Chrome; no free explorer API) — that is the main open gap.

findings.claim: SPEC: ERC-8183 'Agentic Commerce' is a real EIP — Status Draft, Standards Track/ERC, Created 2026-02-25, Requires EIP-20.
findings.detail: Fetched from eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8183. Front matter: Title 'Agentic Commerce'; Description 'Job escrow with evaluator attestation for agent commerce.'; Authors Davide Crapis, Bryan Lim, Tay Weixiong, Chooi Zuhwa; discussions-to https://ethereum-magicians.org/t/erc-8183-agentic-commerce/27902; Status Draft; Type Standards Track; Category ERC; Created 2026-02-25; Requires: EIP-20. The file is also present in the ethereum/ERCs repo at ERCS/erc-8183.md (fetched successfully). NOTE: the exact last-commit date on the ERCs repo was NOT retrieved (GitHub raw does not expose it) — see gaps. 'Requires: EIP-20' is new relative to the prior research and confirms the escrow is ERC-20-denominated at the spec level, not native-coin.

findings.claim: SPEC: the lifecycle is createJob → setProvider/setBudget → fund → submit → complete|reject, plus claimRefund on expiry; three roles (client, provider, evaluator); terminal states are Completed, Rejected, Expired.
findings.detail: Role gating per the spec's transition table: Open→Funded by the client (provider must be set, budget matches expected); Open→Rejected by the client only while Open (this is the client's only unilateral exit); Funded→Submitted by the provider; Funded/Submitted→Completed by the evaluator; Funded/Submitted→Rejected by the evaluator; Funded/Submitted→Expired by anyone once block.timestamp >= expiredAt. Key asymmetry the spec calls out explicitly: 'Once Funded, only the evaluator may reject; clients cannot withdraw' — this protects a provider who has already started work. Completed, Rejected and Expired are terminal. Fees (platform + evaluator) are configurable and deducted only on completion.

findings.claim: SPEC: escrow is a single ERC-20 token; refund after expiry is permissionless and deliberately not hookable.
findings.detail: Quoted from the spec: 'Payment SHALL use a single ERC-20 token (global for the contract or specified at creation).' On expiry: 'When block.timestamp >= job.expiredAt, anyone (or client) may call claimRefund(jobId); contract sets state to Expired and refunds client.' The spec notes refunds after expiry are deliberately NOT hookable, so a malicious or reverting hook cannot trap escrowed funds — this is the single most important safety property to preserve in any fork. Errors defined include ExpiryTooShort() (there is a minimum expiry) and HookNotWhitelisted() (hooks are an allowlist, not arbitrary). Hooks are optional per job and run beforeAction/afterAction around the mutating calls.

findings.claim: SPEC: the evaluator is a single address fixed at job creation — it is NOT elected, staked, or sampled — and settlement depends entirely on it.
findings.detail: 'Single address per job, set at creation. When status is Submitted, only the evaluator MAY call complete or reject.' The evaluator may be the client itself (self-evaluation) or an external contract performing automated checks. What it attests is a bytes32 `reason` passed to complete()/reject() — an opaque evidence pointer (hash/CID), not structured data; there is no on-chain scoring. The spec is candid that 'evaluator trust is paramount' and pushes reputation out of scope: implementations SHOULD use reputation systems for high-value jobs. There is no on-chain dispute or appeal path in the standard — expiry is the only non-evaluator escape, and it always refunds the client. Any arbitration layer (e.g. APEX's OptimisticPolicy) sits behind the evaluator address, not inside the standard.

findings.claim: SPEC: ERC-8004 is RECOMMENDED, not required — 8183 has no hard dependency on 8004 identity.
findings.detail: 'For on-chain reputation and trust relationships between agents, implementations are RECOMMENDED to integrate with ERC-8004 (Trustless Agents)', with reputation signals tied to job outcomes (Completed, Rejected, Expired). Requires: is EIP-20 only — ERC-8004 is NOT in the requires list. Job participants are plain `address` fields (client, provider, evaluator); there is no agentId, no registry lookup, and no identity resolution in the interface. So 8183 composes with 8004 by convention (map an address to an 8004 agent off-chain or in a hook) rather than by type. ERC-2771 meta-transactions are also supported: implementations should use _msgSender() rather than msg.sender for role checks, which is what makes gasless agent-initiated jobs possible.

findings.claim: DEPLOYED: all four README addresses hold code on BSC mainnet (chain 56). Verified by eth_getCode against https://bsc-dataseed.binance.org.
findings.detail: 0xEa4DAa3100A767e86FDed867729ae7446476EBA6 and 0x51895229E12F9876011789B04f8698af06cCD6DA are both ERC-1967 proxies (bytecode begins with the 0x360894a13ba1a3210667c828492db98dca3e2076cc3735a920a3ca505d382bbc implementation slot). eth_getStorageAt on that slot gives implementations: AgenticCommerce → 0xd5f9b570c96b5d67702d508c0bfb8b3b09209787; EvaluatorRouter → 0xf0cf8f47e5c035f16247ff16e9f367e477ee5007. 0x9C01845705b3078Aa2e8cfF7520a6376FD766dE5 (OptimisticPolicy) is a plain non-proxy contract, 4414 bytes. 0xcE24439F2D9C6a2289F741120FE202248B666666 is a *transparent* proxy (exposes 0x5c60da1b implementation() and 0xf851a440 admin()), implementation 0xbef21313c69c009fd7d9510a8d3a481a32473dfc. Read at block 0x6f51571 (116,913,521).

findings.claim: DEPLOYED: the payment token is 'United Stables', symbol 'U', 18 decimals, ~1,019,798,608 total supply — confirming the '$U' belief.
findings.detail: eth_call to 0xcE24439F2D9C6a2289F741120FE202248B666666: name() → 'United Stables'; symbol() → 'U'; decimals() → 18 (0x12); totalSupply() → 0x034b8ec14f421eb4fdb88c00 = 1,019,798,607.908467 U. It is upgradeable behind a transparent proxy — the admin can swap token logic, which is a real counterparty risk to note for an escrow denomination. Sourcify reports this address as verified with BOTH creationMatch and runtimeMatch = exact_match, verifiedAt 2026-03-18T13:17:31Z (matchId 23841599). The AgenticCommerce contract's paymentToken() returns exactly this address, so the escrow asset is U and nothing else — there is no per-job token selection in this deployment.

findings.claim: DEPLOYED: AgenticCommerceUpgradeable really implements ERC-8183 — its runtime bytecode contains the exact keccak selectors for createJob, setBudget, submit, complete, reject, claimRefund, getJob.
findings.detail: Selectors extracted from the implementation runtime code at 0xd5f9b570… and matched against locally computed keccak256: 0x41528812 createJob(address,address,uint256,string,address); 0xdd4ae9d4 setBudget(uint256,uint256,bytes); 0x9e63798d submit(uint256,bytes32,bytes); 0xd75bbdf3 complete(uint256,bytes32,bytes); 0x41dd26f5 reject(uint256,bytes32,bytes); 0x5b7baf64 claimRefund(uint256); 0xbf22c457 getJob(uint256); 0x180aedf3 jobs(uint256); 0x3013ce29 paymentToken(); 0x50355d76 jobCounter(); 0xe138818c platformTreasury(); 0xabe685cd BP_DENOMINATOR(). Ops surface: Ownable2Step (owner/pendingOwner/acceptOwnership/transferOwnership), Pausable (pause/unpause/paused) and UUPS (proxiableUUID, upgradeToAndCall, UPGRADE_INTERFACE_VERSION), initialize(address,address,address). owner() = 0x5057b09a4b510ccaf7e3fb3038ba60713e62b1fc. So a single owner can pause the escrow and upgrade the logic.

findings.claim: DEPLOYED ≠ SPEC: the live fund() and setProvider() signatures differ from the EIP text. Build against the deployed ABI.
findings.detail: The spec lists `fund(uint256 jobId, bytes calldata optParams)` and `setProvider(uint256 jobId, address provider_)`. The deployed implementation instead carries 0xd2e13f50 = fund(uint256,uint256,bytes) — an explicit amount argument — and 0xc9a84bb9 = setProvider(uint256,address,bytes). Neither spec-form selector (0xe25ba707 fund(uint256,bytes), 0xd0fae591 setProvider(uint256,address)) appears in the bytecode. Practical consequence: an integrator generating a client from the EIP's Solidity will get a 'function does not exist' fallback revert on fund. Six ac_impl selectors remain unresolved (0x4fe11c8b, 0x963913a7, 0xb4d884f6, 0xfabc3329, 0xff54740f, 0x4f4a1777-class) — likely fee setters/getters, since fee logic is in the spec but I could not confirm platformFeeBps()/evaluatorFeeBps() (0x22dcd13e / 0x29bc2981) in the code.

findings.claim: DEPLOYED: the system is live and heavily used — 56,610 jobs created, with a job submitted 2026-08-18T11:54:17Z, the same day as this report.
findings.detail: Job IDs are sequential from 1. Binary search over getJob(uint256) (empty struct = not yet created) puts the highest existing job at 56610; getJob(56611) returns an all-zero struct. Job 56610: client 0x7545e5c647880bf16558fdfcda892487dfffe522, provider 0xfaf0ffd121947b9ee3920fa0cfbf9eeeb0acbf7f, evaluator 0x51895229… (the EvaluatorRouter), budget 0.1 U, expiredAt 2026-08-27T11:53:41Z, status 2 (Submitted), submitted-at 2026-08-18T11:54:17Z, deliverable hash 0xb3cad69bd348fab4657d…. Job 56609 is status 1 (Funded). Earliest observed on-chain timestamp is job 5's submit at 2026-05-19T13:58:25Z, so the system has been in production since at least mid-May 2026. Typical budgets seen: 0.1 U, 1e6 wei (dust test), 0.01 U, 9.8 U — i.e. micro-payments.

findings.claim: DEPLOYED: EvaluatorRouterUpgradeable is simultaneously the named evaluator on nearly every job AND the ERC-8183 hook — it implements beforeAction/afterAction and routes to per-job policy contracts.
findings.detail: Selectors in impl 0xf0cf8f47…: 0xdc08fb1d beforeAction(uint256,bytes4,bytes); 0xa3fe4783 afterAction(uint256,bytes4,bytes); 0xa35634b9 jobPolicy(uint256); 0x912955fd commerce(); 0x2761a48b setCommerce(address); 0x01ffc9a7 supportsInterface(bytes4) — matching the spec's `interface IACPHook is IERC165`. Plus Ownable2Step + Pausable + UUPS + initialize(address,address). On the job structs read from chain, the evaluator field equals 0x51895229… for jobs 1,2,10,20,50,100,500,56609,56610; job 5 instead used 0x7e66aebb2f1db6040bd7a931d31b734406aaeb13, so per-job evaluators are possible. Architecturally: ERC-8183 keeps 'one trusted evaluator address'; APEX satisfies that with a router that then delegates the actual accept/reject decision to a swappable policy contract per job.

findings.claim: DEPLOYED: OptimisticPolicy at 0x9C0184… is an optimistic-acceptance + voter-dispute module, not an escrow.
findings.detail: Resolved selectors: 0xe57deb39 check(uint256,bytes) — the policy hook the router calls; 0x117f5f92 disputeWindow(); 0x86d6282c dispute(uint256); 0x43859632 hasVoted(uint256,address); 0xa7771ee3 isVoter(address); 0xf4ab9adf addVoter(address); 0x86c1ff68 removeVoter(address); 0xf887ea40 router(); 0x912955fd commerce(); plus an admin path (0xf851a440 admin(), 0x26782247 pendingAdmin(), 0x75829def transferAdmin(address), 0x0e18b681 acceptAdmin()). Semantics implied by the shape: a submission is optimistically accepted once disputeWindow elapses unless a permissioned voter calls dispute(). Note the voter set is admin-curated (addVoter/removeVoter) — this is a permissioned committee, not open staking, so trust collapses to the policy admin plus the router owner. Ten policy selectors remain unresolved; treat the exact dispute-resolution and payout path as unconfirmed.

findings.claim: DEPLOYED: the live Job struct has more fields than the ERC-8183 struct — a hook/settler address, an extra timestamp, and a bytes32 deliverable are all returned by getJob.
findings.detail: Decoding the raw getJob(uint256) return (a single dynamic tuple), the field order observed is: uint256 id; address client; address provider; address evaluator; string description (head offset 0x160); uint256 budget; uint256 expiredAt; uint8 status; address hook-or-settler; uint256 timestamp (0 until submit — reads as submittedAt); bytes32 deliverable. The spec's `Job` has only id/client/provider/evaluator/description/budget/expiredAt/status/hook. Status values observed in the wild: 0 Open, 1 Funded, 2 Submitted, 3 Completed — matching the spec enum ordering. The 9th field equals the router address on router-evaluated jobs and equals the evaluator on job 5, so 'hook' vs 'settledBy' is not distinguishable from bytecode alone — do not rely on my field name for slot 8/9 without the verified source.

findings.claim: UNVERIFIED: BscScan source-verification status, contract names as displayed, creator address and creation dates could NOT be obtained. The README's claims on those points remain unchecked.
findings.detail: bscscan.com returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch, and a headless Chrome session sat on the Cloudflare 'Just a moment…' interstitial through ~40s of polling. api.bscscan.com V1 is retired ('use Etherscan API V2'), Etherscan V2 needs a key not present in this repo, api.routescan.io answers 'chain not supported' for 56, and no Blockscout instance for BSC responded. Sourcify has NO record for 0xEa4DAa31…, 0xd5f9b570… or 0x9C0184… (match:null) — that is NOT evidence they are unverified on BscScan, only that they were never pushed to Sourcify. Historical eth_getCode is also unavailable: every free BSC RPC tried is pruned ('missing trie node') or gated, so creation blocks could not be binary-searched either. The earliest hard on-chain evidence of life is 2026-05-19.

interfaces.name: ERC-8183 core interface (SPEC, verbatim from eips.ethereum.org)
ERC-8183 events and errors (SPEC)
IACPHook (SPEC, verbatim)
ERC-8183 state machine — transition / caller / condition (SPEC)
interfaces.body:
| Transition                    | Caller    | Condition                                   |
|-------------------------------|-----------|---------------------------------------------|
| Open -> Funded                | Client    | Provider must be set; budget matches expected|
| Open -> Rejected              | Client    | Only while in Open                          |
| Funded -> Submitted           | Provider  | Job is Funded                               |
| Funded/Submitted -> Completed | Evaluator | Job is Submitted                            |
| Funded/Submitted -> Rejected  | Evaluator | Before or after submission                  |
| Funded/Submitted -> Expired   | Anyone    | block.timestamp >= expiredAt                |

Terminal states: Completed, Rejected, Expired.
Expiry path (claimRefund) is deliberately NOT hookable, so a hook cannot
block recovery of escrowed funds.
Fees (platform + evaluator) are deducted only on Completed.

Resolve with an Etherscan V2 key: https://api.etherscan.io/v2/api?chainid=56&module=contract&action=getsourcecode&address=0xEa4DAa3100A767e86FDed867729ae7446476EBA6

Contract creation transactions, creator addresses and deployment dates for all four addresses are UNKNOWN. Free BSC RPCs are pruned ('missing trie node' on historical eth_getCode), so a creation-block binary search was impossible. Needs an archive node or an explorer getcontractcreation call.

The exact 'last commit date' of ERCS/erc-8183.md in the ethereum/ERCs repo was not retrieved — raw.githubusercontent.com does not expose commit metadata. Query https://api.github.com/repos/ethereum/ERCs/commits?path=ERCS/erc-8183.md&per_page=1 to get it.

Fee mechanics in the deployed contract are unconfirmed: neither platformFeeBps() (0x22dcd13e) nor evaluatorFeeBps() (0x29bc2981) matched the bytecode, though platformTreasury() and BP_DENOMINATOR() are present. Five AgenticCommerce selectors remain unresolved (0x4fe11c8b, 0x963913a7, 0xb4d884f6, 0xfabc3329, 0xff54740f) and likely cover fee config.

Ten of OptimisticPolicy's selectors and six of EvaluatorRouter's are unresolved, so the precise dispute-resolution and settlement path (how check() returns, what quorum applies, who pays out on a successful dispute) is inferred from the resolved names only, not read from source.

The spec quotes on escrow asset, timeout semantics, evaluator role and ERC-8004 were returned by a summarizing fetch and are reported as quotes; a byte-exact re-read of the Specification and Rationale sections is advisable before quoting them in a public document.

The two extra Job struct fields observed on-chain (slot 8 address, slot 9 timestamp) are named 'hook/settler' and 'submittedAt' by inference from behaviour across jobs 1/5/10/20/100/500/56609/56610, not from verified source.

No ERC-8004 registry interaction was observed on-chain in this deployment: job participants are plain addresses and no 8004 registry address surfaced in the selector maps. Whether APEX resolves 8004 identities off-chain is unknown.

The U token (0xcE2443...666666) is behind a transparent upgradeable proxy; its admin address was not read (call admin() from a non-admin caller reverts on OZ TransparentUpgradeableProxy — read EIP-1967 admin slot 0xb53127684a568b3173ae13b9f8a6016e243e63b6e8ee1178d6a717850b5d6103 instead).
aiki_implications: ERC-8183 is a legitimate, live standard on BSC with 56,610 jobs and same-day activity — not a paper spec. If AiKi is doing agent commerce on chain 56, implementing the ERC-8183 job interface is the interoperability path of least resistance, and APEX is the incumbent to interop with or differentiate from.

Integrate against the DEPLOYED ABI, not the EIP text. fund is fund(uint256,uint256,bytes) and setProvider is setProvider(uint256,address,bytes) on chain; codegen from the published Solidity will revert. Pin selectors 0xd2e13f50 and 0xc9a84bb9 in any integration test.

The escrow asset is U (United Stables, 0xcE24439F2D9C6a2289F741120FE202248B666666, 18 decimals) and it is itself upgradeable behind a transparent proxy. Denominating AiKi escrow in U inherits that upgrade authority as counterparty risk; a stablecoin choice with immutable logic, or a per-job token parameter, is a defensible differentiator.

ERC-8183's trust model collapses to one address per job. APEX papers over this with EvaluatorRouter -> per-job policy, but the OptimisticPolicy voter set is admin-curated (addVoter/removeVoter behind admin()). If AiKi's pitch is trust, the credible wedge is a policy contract with staked/slashable or sampled evaluators that still presents as a single evaluator address to 8183 — the standard permits exactly that substitution with no fork.

The hook interface is the real extension point. IACPHook.beforeAction/afterAction with the calling selector gives AiKi a place to write reputation, ERC-8004 attestations, or risk checks without touching escrow. Note hooks are allowlisted (HookNotWhitelisted) and the expiry/refund path is intentionally non-hookable — preserve that property or you reintroduce fund-trapping.

ERC-8004 is only RECOMMENDED by 8183 and there is no identity type in the interface (participants are raw addresses). AiKi has open ground to define the address -> agent-identity binding — doing it inside a hook, emitting on completion, is the composable way and does not require a new ERC.

Only two terminal outcomes move money: Completed pays the provider, Expired refunds the client. Rejected has no payout path defined in the transition table beyond leaving escrow untouched — clarify refund-on-reject semantics against the verified source before designing any AiKi settlement that assumes rejection returns funds.

Operational reality to match: the live escrow is Ownable2Step + Pausable + UUPS under a single EOA-looking owner (0x5057b09a...). A pause halts all commerce and an upgrade can rewrite settlement. If AiKi wants to claim stronger execution guarantees, a timelock or multisig on the upgrade path is a concrete, verifiable differentiator a reviewer can check on-chain.

Observed budgets are micro (0.1 U, 0.01 U, dust). Design AiKi's fee and gas model for sub-dollar jobs on BSC; a per-job on-chain arbitration round would exceed the job value at these sizes, which is precisely why APEX chose optimistic acceptance.
